$$
\begin{aligned}x & =5{b}_{1}-2{b}_{2} \\  & =-2{b}_{2}+5{b}_{1} \\  & =2(-{b}_{2})-\frac{5}{3}(-3{b}_{1}) \\  & =2{c}_{1}-\frac{5}{3}{c}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ![](images/f6/f6a8d41276d74ce726301f3cc83d87542d49115eb46cf0f836d20816cd660168.svg)" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186119824 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-be777f36-f8c5-5b1e-a52c-750939157337"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186119635 :question/problem "Let $\mathcal{B}= \left\{ \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2,\mathbf{b}_3 \right\}$ be a basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$ and ![](images/19/191549b963b841cb97bbad9b6c65019d913cc148ed466d3c026cc27eccff1d8d.svg) What are the coordinates of $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}= \left\{ \mathbf{c}_1, \mathbf{c}_2, \mathbf{c}_3 \right\},$ where $\mathbf{c}_1 = -3\mathbf{b}_2,$ $\mathbf{c}_2=-\mathbf{b}_3,$ and $\mathbf{c}_3 = -4\mathbf{b}_1?$" :question/worked-solution "Since ![](images/33/334e52d3fd172cadf353bd6b3d6f3fe66eb0c722320da14ce6fd11b66cdca79a.svg) we can write $\mathbf{x}$ in terms of the vectors $\mathbf c_1, \mathbf c_2,$ and $\mathbf c_3,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-2{b}_{1}-3{b}_{2}+5{b}_{3} \\  & =-3{b}_{2}+5{b}_{3}-2{b}_{1} \\  & =(-3{b}_{2})-5(-{b}_{3})+\frac{1}{2}(-4{b}_{1}) \\  & ={c}_{1}-5{c}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{c}_{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ![](images/9a/9a0eec63eca72981c016e4c504a49d249b6514e5e4f12e77e7d721282b7b24bb.svg)" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186119825 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-07f1e9fd-ac52-515f-8ec2-7b10b57c07ec" "question-f46f0e34-3d5c-5e7a-9fb4-690993802dbe"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186119636 :question/problem "Let $\mathcal{B}= \left\{ \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2 \right\}$ be a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and ![](images/e8/e8c67f642148caf84c01b7ee88fe125c4a5ae37ecae313d01d45c277de51d74b.svg) What are the coordinates of $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}= \left\{ \mathbf{c}_1, \mathbf{c}_2 \right\},$ where $\mathbf{c}_1 = \mathbf{b}_2-\mathbf{b}_1$ and $\mathbf{c}_2 = 2\mathbf{b}_1 - 3\mathbf{b}_2?$" :question/worked-solution "We are given that

$$
{\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}={b}_{2}-{b}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}=2{b}_{1}-3{b}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we express the $\mathbf{b}$'s in terms of $\mathbf{c}$'s. Multiplying the first equation by $2$ and adding the equations, we get 

$$
2\mathbf{c}_1+\mathbf{c}_2 = -\mathbf{b}_2
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\mathbf{b}_2 = -2\mathbf{c}_1-\mathbf{c}_2.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\mathbf{c}_1 = \left( -2\mathbf{c}_1-\mathbf{c}_2 \right) - \mathbf{b}_1
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\mathbf{b}_1 = -3\mathbf{c}_1-\mathbf{c}_2.
$$

Since ![](images/0e/0e283c9948eacf3e231eef3a3feb355c33f20c3dbfd89e97c530331758af34ad.svg) we can write the vector $\mathbf{x}$ in terms of the vectors $\mathbf c_1$ and $\mathbf c_2,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={b}_{1}-3{b}_{2} \\  & =(-3{c}_{1}-{c}_{2})-3(-2{c}_{1}-{c}_{2}) \\  & =-3{c}_{1}-{c}_{2}+6{c}_{1}+3{c}_{2} \\  & =3{c}_{1}+2{c}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ![](images/d8/d8d25ca46df4435c67e7c23e61851e2acd4826b0b2d99d9b54de8b6f2c37ee94.svg)" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-1819c1f8-4cd2-5652-80f1-d185af0479c5" :question/id #uuid "1819c1f8-4cd2-5652-80f1-d185af0479c5" :question/math-academy-id "q-35260" :question/problem "Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ be a basis of ${R}^{2}$ and $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -5\end{aligned}].$ What are the coordinates of $x$ relative to the basis $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2}},$ where ${c}_{1}=5{b}_{2}$ and ${c}_{2}=-3{b}_{1}?$" :question/worked-solution "Since $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -5\end{aligned}]$, we can write $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={b}_{1}-5{b}_{2} \\  & =-5{b}_{2}+{b}_{1} \\  & =-(5{b}_{2})-(-{b}_{1}) \\  & =-(5{b}_{2})-\frac{1}{3}(-3{b}_{1}) \\  & =-{c}_{1}-\frac{1}{3}{c}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}].$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d0279881-209b-5f19-932e-f90a7a749d9f"] $$
{\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}={b}_{1}+{b}_{2} \\ {c}_{2}={b}_{2}-{b}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}=2{b}_{2}\,⟹\,{b}_{2}=\frac{1}{2}{c}_{1}+\frac{1}{2}{c}_{2}.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
{c}_{1}={b}_{1}+(\frac{1}{2}{c}_{1}+\frac{1}{2}{c}_{2})\,⟹\,{b}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{c}_{1}-\frac{1}{2}{c}_{2}.
$$

Since $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$, we can write the vector $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =7{b}_{1}+{b}_{2} \\  & =7(\frac{1}{2}{c}_{1}-\frac{1}{2}{c}_{2})+(\frac{1}{2}{c}_{1}+\frac{1}{2}{c}_{2}) \\  & =\frac{7}{2}{c}_{1}-\frac{7}{2}{c}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{c}_{1}+\frac{1}{2}{c}_{2} \\  & =4{c}_{1}-3{c}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -3\end{aligned}].$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d8e25391-7c4e-5c7c-8ae1-5b47ead04007"] :db/ensure $$
{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}={b}_{1}\,⟹\,{b}_{1}={c}_{1}+{c}_{2}.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
{c}_{1}=2({c}_{1}+{c}_{2})-{b}_{2}\,⟹\,{b}_{2}={c}_{1}+2{c}_{2}.
$$

Since $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2\end{aligned}]$, we can write the vector $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =4{b}_{1}-2{b}_{2} \\  & =4({c}_{1}+{c}_{2})-2({c}_{1}+2{c}_{2}) \\  & =4{c}_{1}+4{c}_{2}-2{c}_{1}-4{c}_{2} \\  & =2{c}_{1}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-6f810d6a-b71d-5aa6-a732-e9b3cdb4d3fc"] :db/ensure $$
{\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}={b}_{1}+{b}_{2} \\ {c}_{2}={b}_{2}-{b}_{1}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

Since $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$, we can write the vector $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =7{b}_{1}+{b}_{2} \\  & =7(\frac{1}{2}{c}_{1}-\frac{1}{2}{c}_{2})+(\frac{1}{2}{c}_{1}+\frac{1}{2}{c}_{2}) \\  & =\frac{7}{2}{c}_{1}-\frac{7}{2}{c}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{c}_{1}+\frac{1}{2}{c}_{2} \\  & =4{c}_{1}-3{c}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

How can we find the coordinates of $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{B}?$

Since ![](images/3e/3e330c07260a16bc76853ca1d275bbd9759f60179dce22500ee6dd38f326ca20.svg) we can write the vector $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal B$ as follows:

$$

$$
{\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}=2{b}_{1}-{b}_{2} \\ {c}_{2}=-{b}_{1}+{b}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we express the $b$'s in terms of $c$'s. Adding the equations, we get 

$$
{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}={b}_{1}\,⟹\,{b}_{1}={c}_{1}+{c}_{2}.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
{c}_{1}=2({c}_{1}+{c}_{2})-{b}_{2}\,⟹\,{b}_{2}={c}_{1}+2{c}_{2}.
$$

Since $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2\end{aligned}]$, we can write the vector $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =4{b}_{1}-2{b}_{2} \\  & =4({c}_{1}+{c}_{2})-2({c}_{1}+2{c}_{2}) \\  & =4{c}_{1}+4{c}_{2}-2{c}_{1}-4{c}_{2} \\  & =2{c}_{1}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$"] ["question-07f1e9fd-ac52-515f-8ec2-7b10b57c07ec" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["question-f46f0e34-3d5c-5e7a-9fb4-690993802dbe" :question/math-academy-id "q-81230"] ["question-f46f0e34-3d5c-5e7a-9fb4-690993802dbe" :question/problem "Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ be a basis of ${c}_{2}={b}_{2}-{b}_{1}?$"] ["question-f46f0e34-3d5c-5e7a-9fb4-690993802dbe" :question/worked-solution "We are given that

$$
{\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}={b}_{1}+{b}_{2} \\ {c}_{2}={b}_{2}-{b}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we express the $b$'s in terms of $c$'s. By adding the equations, we get 

$$
{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}=2{b}_{2}\,⟹\,{b}_{2}=\frac{1}{2}{c}_{1}+\frac{1}{2}{c}_{2}.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
{c}_{1}={b}_{1}+(\frac{1}{2}{c}_{1}+\frac{1}{2}{c}_{2})\,⟹\,{b}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{c}_{1}-\frac{1}{2}{c}_{2}.
$$

Since $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$, we can write the vector $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =7{b}_{1}+{b}_{2} \\  & =7(\frac{1}{2}{c}_{1}-\frac{1}{2}{c}_{2})+(\frac{1}{2}{c}_{1}+\frac{1}{2}{c}_{2}) \\  & =\frac{7}{2}{c}_{1}-\frac{7}{2}{c}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{c}_{1}+\frac{1}{2}{c}_{2} \\  & =4{c}_{1}-3{c}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -3\end{aligned}].$"] ["question-f46f0e34-3d5c-5e7a-9fb4-690993802dbe" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] Now, let $\mathcal{B}= \left\{ \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2 \right\}$ be another basis of $\mathbb{R}^2,$ such that

$$
\mathbf{b}_1 = \mathbf{c}_2 \quad \textrm{and} \quad \mathbf{b}_2 = -2\mathbf{c}_1.
$$

How can we find the coordinates of $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{B}?$

Since ![](images/3e/3e330c07260a16bc76853ca1d275bbd9759f60179dce22500ee6dd38f326ca20.svg) we can write the vector $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal B$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2{c}_{1}-{c}_{2} \\  & =-{c}_{2}+2{c}_{1} \\  & =-({c}_{2})-(-2{c}_{1}) \\  & =-{b}_{1}-{b}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ![](images/5d/5d39ae32e2bad5125e6d7cf8ba7b943f2c926e1f1d6525ce019fd9a40c263bce.svg)"] [17592186121070 :tutorial/content "Let $\mathcal{B}= \left\{ \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2 \right\}$ be a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and ![](images/be/bec3577dd261660f2545adb66b9c26fbb520ea60aa6b0337094347dbc1937ff4.svg) What are the coordinates of $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}= \left\{ \mathbf{c}_1, \mathbf{c}_2 \right\},$ where $\mathbf{b}_1 = 2\mathbf{c}_1-\mathbf{c}_2$ and $\mathbf{b}_2 = \mathbf{c}_1+\mathbf{c}_2?$
